Baby & Child

Potty Training: When and How to Start

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Few parenting milestones come with as much unsolicited advice as potty training. The truth is refreshingly simple: children train fastest and happiest when they are actually ready, the process stays calm, and accidents are treated as information rather than failure. Here is how to do that, step by step.

Readiness matters more than age

Most children show readiness somewhere between 18 months and 3 years, with many landing around age two to two and a half: but the age matters far less than the signs. Starting before readiness does not produce an early finisher; it usually just produces a longer, more frustrating process.

Look for a cluster of signals: staying dry for two hours or more, noticing or announcing a wet or dirty diaper, hiding to poop, interest in the toilet or in your bathroom trips, ability to pull pants up and down, following simple instructions, and (importantly) willingness. A child who firmly refuses is telling you the answer for now.

You do not need every sign, but several together suggest the window is open. If in doubt, wait a few weeks; readiness has a way of announcing itself.

Gear and groundwork

Keep equipment simple: a floor potty (less intimidating, feet on the ground) or a seat reducer plus a step stool for the big toilet: many families have both. Add easy-off clothes: elastic waists are potty-training gold, and overalls are the enemy.

Prepare the mind as well as the bathroom. In the weeks before starting, read picture books about the potty, let your child watch family members use the toilet, and let them sit on the potty fully clothed just to get acquainted. Let them pick out underwear: ownership is motivating.

Then choose a reasonably calm stretch of life to begin. Launching potty training the same week as a house move or a new sibling stacks the odds against everyone.

A calm step-by-step approach

Start with routine sits at high-probability moments (after waking, after meals, before bath) keeping them short and pressure-free, a couple of minutes with a book. Whether anything happens or not, the sit itself is the win at first.

When your child starts producing on the potty, move to underwear during the day and offer regular, matter-of-fact reminders ("Time to try the potty"). Some families do a concentrated few days at home; others go gradually over weeks. Both work: pick what suits your child and your calendar.

Celebrate successes warmly but briefly (enthusiastic praise, a sticker if that motivates your child) and keep the overall temperature low. A potty that becomes a stage show can start to feel like pressure, and pressure is the main thing that stalls training.

Accidents without shame

Accidents are not a bug in potty training; they are the curriculum. A small bladder plus a fascinating game equals a puddle: that is physiology, not defiance. Respond with a shrug and a script: "Pee goes in the potty. Let us get dry clothes."

Never scold, punish, or shame an accident. Shame does not speed up training: it reliably slows it down, and it is a particular culprit in children who start withholding poop, which creates real problems. Your calm is the most useful tool you own.

Involving your child matter-of-factly in cleanup (fetching dry clothes, helping wipe the floor) builds responsibility without blame. Then move on completely.

Nighttime comes later

Daytime and nighttime dryness are different systems on different timelines. Staying dry overnight depends on bladder maturity and hormone changes that a child cannot control or be trained into, so keep diapers or training pants at night without a hint of judgment.

Many children stay in night protection for months or years after daytime training, and occasional bedwetting remains common and normal well into the school years. When you notice consistently dry mornings for a week or two, that is the sign to try underwear at night. If bedwetting persists past around age six or seven, or worries you, your pediatrician is the right person to ask.

Regressions are normal

A fully trained child who suddenly starts having accidents again is frustrating but common. The usual suspects are life changes (a new sibling, starting daycare, moving, illness, or any stretch of stress) and sometimes simple absorption in play.

Respond by going back to basics calmly: more reminders, scheduled potty sits, zero drama about accidents, and a little extra connection, since regressions often coincide with a child needing reassurance. Most regressions resolve in a few weeks with boring consistency.

If a regression persists, or you notice pain with peeing, constipation, or poop withholding, check in with your pediatrician: occasionally there is a physical cause that is easy to treat once found.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Toilet learning works best when a child can notice the urge, communicate it, reach the toilet, manage clothing with help, and show interest. Readiness varies, and pressure or punishment can make the process harder.

Use a calm routine, easy clothing, praise for participation, and neutral responses to accidents. Constipation, pain, stool withholding, or regression may need healthcare guidance.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to notice readiness, routines, and constipation patterns without turning the tracker into a reward or punishment system.

When to seek help

Contact a healthcare professional for painful urination or stool, blood, persistent constipation, marked thirst, or a sudden loss of previously established skills.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Potty Training
  • CDC — Essentials for Parenting Toddlers and Preschoolers

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Readiness signs (dry stretches, awareness, interest, willingness) matter more than any target age.
  • Prepare with simple gear, easy-off clothes, potty books, and a calm week to start.
  • Keep the process low-pressure: routine sits, matter-of-fact reminders, brief warm praise.
  • Treat accidents as information, never with shame: calm cleanup, dry clothes, move on.
  • Nighttime dryness comes on its own later, and regressions are a normal detour, not a failure.

Frequently asked questions

How long does potty training take?

It varies widely: some ready children get the hang of daytime training in days, others take weeks or a few months. Readiness at the start is the biggest predictor. If there is no progress after a few weeks, pause without drama and try again later.

Should I use rewards like stickers or treats?

Small, immediate rewards like stickers work well for many children as a short-term boost, and interest naturally fades once the skill is routine. Keep rewards low-key and pair them with praise: the goal is a child who feels proud, not one performing for payment.

My child refuses to poop on the potty but pees fine. What now?

This is very common: pooping on the potty feels different and can worry children. Keep it pressure-free, since fear can lead to withholding and constipation, which makes everything harder. Some families allow a diaper for poops temporarily while staying relaxed. If withholding or constipation develops, talk to your pediatrician.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
